mcqs.stem: Q7.2. Which best defines an enzyme?
rationales: Some enzymes break down food, but this is not a complete definition.
A hormone is not the definition of an enzyme.
Correct: an enzyme is a protein that speeds up reactions.
Energy storage is not the main role described by this definition.

rationales: Above its optimum, activity may fall rather than keep increasing.

rationales: Correct: an enzyme’s active site has a shape that fits particular substrate(s).

rationales: Correct: activity usually increases with temperature up to the optimum.
Activity does not always decrease as temperature rises; it can first increase.

More hydrogen ions do not necessarily make the enzyme work faster; this pH is far from its optimum.

written.text: Q7.1. Define metabolism. Differentiate between catabolism and anabolism.
written.finalAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions taking place in a living organism. Catabolism breaks down complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy; anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and requires energy.

rubric.why: The definition identifies what metabolism includes.
rubric.how: State that metabolism is the sum of the chemical reactions in an organism.

rubric.why: This distinguishes breakdown reactions from building reactions.
rubric.how: Say that catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy.

rubric.why: Anabolism is the opposite type of metabolic reaction.
rubric.how: Say that anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and requires energy.

rubric.why: A clear contrast is needed to differentiate the two processes.
rubric.how: Include both processes and their contrasting direction or energy requirement.

modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions taking place in a living organism.
Catabolism breaks down complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy.
Anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and requires energy.
Thus, catabolism is breakdown, whereas anabolism is building.

written.text: Q7.2. Which type of metabolism demands input of energy? Give an example.
written.finalAnswer: Anabolism demands input of energy. For example, the synthesis of proteins from amino acids.

rubric.why: Identifying the correct type of metabolism earns the first mark.
rubric.how: State that anabolism demands energy input.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates understanding of energy-requiring synthesis.
rubric.how: Give protein synthesis from amino acids or another valid anabolic example.

modelAnswer: Anabolism demands input of energy.
For example, amino acids are joined to form proteins.
Final answer: Anabolism; protein synthesis from amino acids.

written.text: Q7.3. Define an enzyme. What is its role in metabolism?
written.finalAnswer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed. Enzymes catalyse metabolic reactions.

rubric.why: The definition must identify an enzyme as a catalyst and its effect on reaction rate.
rubric.how: Define it as a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up reactions.

rubric.why: This explains how enzymes contribute to metabolism.
rubric.how: Explain that enzymes catalyse metabolic reactions.

modelAnswer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed.
Enzymes catalyse the chemical reactions of metabolism.

written.text: Q7.4. What is the active site of enzyme? State its importance in enzyme specificity.
written.finalAnswer: The active site is the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction occurs. Its shape fits particular substrate(s), giving the enzyme specificity.

rubric.why: The active site must be located by its role in substrate binding.
rubric.how: Say that it is the enzyme region where the substrate binds.

rubric.why: The fit between active site and substrate explains enzyme specificity.
rubric.how: Link the active-site shape to fitting a particular substrate.

modelAnswer: The active site is the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction occurs.
Its shape fits particular substrates, so an enzyme acts specifically on its substrate.

written.text: Q7.5. Provide an example of a specific enzyme-substrate pair.

rubric.why: The enzyme must be correctly identified.
rubric.how: Give a valid enzyme, such as amylase.

rubric.why: The matching substrate completes the specific pair.
rubric.how: Pair amylase with starch.

modelAnswer: Amylase acts on starch.
Final answer: Amylase and starch.

written.text: Q7.6. What is the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity?
written.finalAnswer: Increasing substrate concentration increases enzyme activity until the enzyme active sites are saturated; after that, the rate reaches a maximum and does not increase further.

rubric.why: The initial increase in substrate availability raises the reaction rate.
rubric.how: Explain that activity increases as substrate concentration rises.

rubric.why: The rate stops increasing when all available active sites are occupied.
rubric.how: Explain that saturation produces a maximum rate.

modelAnswer: As substrate concentration increases, enzyme activity increases because more substrate molecules can bind to active sites.
When all active sites are occupied, the enzymes are saturated and the rate reaches a maximum.
Further increase in substrate concentration does not increase the rate.

written.text: Q7.7. Provide two examples of enzymes that operate optimally at specific pH.
written.finalAnswer: Pepsin operates optimally at a low, acidic pH, while trypsin operates optimally at a high, alkaline pH.

rubric.why: Pepsin is an example of an enzyme with an acidic pH optimum.
rubric.description: Gives the first enzyme and its optimum.
rubric.how: State that pepsin works best at low or acidic pH.

rubric.why: Trypsin provides a contrasting alkaline pH example.
rubric.description: Gives the second enzyme and its optimum.
rubric.how: State that trypsin works best at high or alkaline pH.

modelAnswer: Pepsin operates optimally at a low, acidic pH.
Trypsin operates optimally at a high, alkaline pH.

written.text: Q7.8. What do you mean by optimum temperature and pH?
written.finalAnswer: The optimum temperature and optimum pH are the temperature and pH at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate.

rubric.why: The optimum temperature is defined by the highest enzyme activity.
rubric.how: State that it is the temperature at which the enzyme works fastest.

rubric.why: The optimum pH is also defined by the highest enzyme activity.
rubric.how: State that it is the pH at which the enzyme works fastest.

modelAnswer: Optimum temperature is the temperature at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate.
Optimum pH is the pH at which an enzyme works at its maximum rate.

written.text: Q7.9. Which type of enzyme inhibitors inhibit the enzymes without attaching to the active site?

rubric.why: This identifies the inhibitor type that binds away from the active site.
rubric.how: Answer non-competitive inhibitors.

modelAnswer: Non-competitive inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site.
Final answer: Non-competitive inhibitors.

written.text: Q7.10. Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive inhibition.
written.finalAnswer: A competitive inhibitor binds to and blocks the active site, competing with the substrate. A non-competitive inhibitor binds at a site other than the active site and changes the enzyme’s shape, reducing its activity.

rubric.why: The active-site competition is the defining feature of competitive inhibition.
rubric.how: State that the inhibitor binds to and blocks the active site.

rubric.why: Binding away from the active site distinguishes non-competitive inhibition.
rubric.how: State that it binds elsewhere and can alter enzyme shape or activity.

modelAnswer: A competitive inhibitor binds to the active site and competes with the substrate for it.
A non-competitive inhibitor binds to a site other than the active site and changes the enzyme’s shape or activity.

written.text: Q7.1. Describe the characteristics of enzymes.
written.finalAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts, primarily proteins. They speed up metabolic reactions without being consumed, are specific because their active sites fit particular substrates, and work best at optimum temperature and pH.

rubric.why: The answer should state the nature of enzymes.
rubric.how: Describe enzymes as mainly proteins and biological catalysts.

rubric.why: Catalysing reactions is their central function.
rubric.how: State that enzymes speed up chemical or metabolic reactions.

rubric.why: Enzymes remain available after catalysing a reaction.
rubric.how: Explain that enzymes are not used up in the reaction.

rubric.why: Specificity and conditions of activity are important characteristics.
rubric.how: Include enzyme specificity or the need for optimum conditions.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts and are primarily proteins.
They speed up chemical reactions, including metabolic reactions.
They are not consumed in the reactions and can be used again.
Enzymes are specific because each active site fits particular substrate(s).
Each enzyme works best at an optimum temperature and pH.

written.text: Q7.2. Describe how temperature extremes can inhibit enzyme activity and lead to enzyme denaturation.
written.finalAnswer: Low temperatures reduce enzyme and substrate movement, so fewer successful collisions occur and activity decreases. Above the optimum temperature, heat changes the enzyme’s shape, including its active site. The substrate no longer fits properly; the enzyme is denatured and its activity is greatly reduced or stops.

rubric.why: Low temperature slows reactions without necessarily denaturing the enzyme.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of low temperature.
rubric.how: Connect reduced molecular movement or collision rate with reduced activity.

rubric.why: The damaging effect is associated with temperatures above the optimum.
rubric.how: State that excessive heat, above the optimum, can alter the enzyme.

rubric.why: A changed active site explains why the substrate cannot bind normally.
rubric.how: State that heat changes the shape of the enzyme or its active site.

rubric.why: The answer must link denaturation to loss of enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Explain that the substrate no longer fits and the enzyme’s activity falls or stops.

modelAnswer: At low temperatures, enzyme and substrate molecules move more slowly.
Fewer successful collisions occur, so enzyme activity decreases.
Above the optimum temperature, excessive heat changes the shape of the enzyme, including its active site.
The substrate can no longer fit properly; the enzyme is denatured and its activity is greatly reduced or stops.

written.text: Q7.3. How does pH affect enzyme activity?
written.finalAnswer: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works fastest. A pH above or below this optimum can change the shape and charge of the active site, making substrate binding less effective and reducing activity. At an extreme pH, the enzyme may be denatured.

rubric.why: The optimum pH is the reference point for the effect of pH.
rubric.how: Say that each enzyme has an optimum pH where activity is greatest.

rubric.why: Activity is affected when conditions move away from the optimum.
rubric.how: State that pH above or below the optimum reduces activity.

rubric.why: The structural change explains the effect on enzyme-substrate binding.
rubric.description: Explains the change to the enzyme.
rubric.how: Describe the active site as changing shape or being altered.

rubric.why: This connects changed pH with reduced reaction rate or denaturation.
rubric.how: Explain that binding and activity fall, and extreme pH may denature the enzyme.

modelAnswer: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works at its maximum rate.
A pH above or below this optimum can change the shape or charge of the enzyme’s active site.
The substrate then binds less effectively, so enzyme activity decreases.
At an extreme pH, the enzyme may become denatured.

written.text: Q7.4. Describe the factors that affect the activity of enzymes.
written.finalAnswer: Enzyme activity is affected by temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors. Activity increases with temperature up to the optimum, but excessive heat can denature the enzyme. Each enzyme has an optimum pH, and a pH away from it can alter the active site. Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate until active sites are saturated. Competitive inhibitors block the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and alter enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Temperature affects reaction rate and can damage enzyme structure.
rubric.how: Mention rising activity to the optimum and reduced activity or denaturation above it.

rubric.why: pH can affect the active site and substrate binding.
rubric.how: State that activity is greatest at an optimum pH and falls away from it.

rubric.why: Substrate concentration changes the number of enzyme-substrate interactions.
rubric.how: Explain the increase up to saturation and the maximum rate.

rubric.why: Competitive inhibition reduces substrate access to the active site.
rubric.how: State that a competitive inhibitor blocks the active site.

rubric.why: Non-competitive inhibition affects the enzyme without occupying the active site.
rubric.how: State that it binds elsewhere and alters enzyme shape or activity.

modelAnswer: Temperature affects enzyme activity: activity usually increases up to the optimum temperature, but excessive heat may denature the enzyme.
Each enzyme has an optimum pH; a pH away from it may alter the active site and reduce activity.
Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate until the active sites become saturated.
A competitive inhibitor blocks the active site and competes with the substrate.
A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme’s shape or activity.

written.text: Q7.5. Compare the Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit models of enzyme action.
written.finalAnswer: In the Lock-and-Key model, the active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate, which fits it like a key in a lock. In the Induced Fit model, the active site is flexible and changes shape as the substrate binds. Both models explain enzyme-substrate specificity and the formation of an enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: A fixed complementary active site is the defining feature of the Lock-and-Key model.
rubric.how: Explain that the substrate fits a fixed-shape active site.

rubric.why: Active-site adjustment distinguishes the Induced Fit model.
rubric.how: State that the active site changes shape as the substrate binds.

rubric.why: Both models explain how enzyme and substrate interact specifically.
rubric.how: Show that the substrate binds to the enzyme’s active site.

rubric.why: Specificity is a key feature common to both explanations.
rubric.how: Mention that both models explain enzyme specificity.

rubric.why: A complete comparison includes the reaction sequence after binding.
rubric.how: Describe formation of the enzyme-substrate complex and release of products, or give an accurate labelled model diagram.

modelAnswer: In the Lock-and-Key model, the enzyme’s active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate.
The substrate fits into this active site like a key fits into a lock.
In the Induced Fit model, the active site is flexible and changes shape as the substrate binds.
Both models show specific substrate binding and formation of an enzyme-substrate complex.
After the reaction, products leave the enzyme and the enzyme can be used again.

Diagram to draw and label: show two side-by-side enzyme models. Label the first “Lock-and-Key”: a fixed active site, a matching substrate, and the enzyme-substrate complex. Label the second “Induced Fit”: an initially flexible active site, the substrate, and the changed active site around the bound substrate. Add arrows showing substrate binding and product release.

examTips: Short questions commonly ask for definitions, examples, the effect of one factor, or a distinction such as competitive versus non-competitive inhibition.
For a definition, include the key terms rather than giving only an example. For enzyme specificity, mention the active site and its fit with the substrate.
Long questions may ask for characteristics, factors affecting activity, or a comparison of the two enzyme-action models.
For a comparison, name both models and state the difference in active-site shape: fixed in Lock-and-Key, changing in Induced Fit.
For temperature and pH questions, state the optimum first, then explain what happens away from it and link the change in shape to reduced substrate binding.
If a diagram is requested for enzyme action, label the enzyme, active site, substrate, enzyme-substrate complex and products; use arrows to show the sequence.

explain.title: Metabolism has two directions
explain.body: Metabolism is the sum of the chemical reactions in a living organism. Catabolism breaks complex molecules down and releases energy. Anabolism builds complex molecules and requires energy.

explain.title: Enzymes are biological catalysts
explain.body: Enzymes are primarily proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being consumed. Their active sites bind particular substrates, which makes enzyme action specific.

explain.title: Enzyme activity depends on conditions
explain.body: Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and optimum pH at which it works fastest. Temperature and pH changes can reduce activity; extreme conditions can change the active site and denature the enzyme.

explain.title: Substrate concentration affects reaction rate
explain.body: As substrate concentration rises, activity increases because more substrate molecules can reach active sites. Once the active sites are saturated, the rate reaches a maximum.

explain.title: Inhibitors reduce enzyme action
explain.body: A competitive inhibitor binds to the active site and competes with the substrate. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and can change the enzyme’s shape or activity.

explain.title: Two models explain enzyme-substrate binding
explain.body: The Lock-and-Key model describes a fixed active site that matches its substrate. The Induced Fit model describes an active site that changes shape as the substrate binds.

mistakes: Do not say enzymes are used up in the reaction; they can be used again.
Do not say enzyme activity always decreases as temperature rises. It usually rises up to the optimum, then may fall as the enzyme denatures.
Do not confuse optimum pH with a pH that suits every enzyme; different enzymes have different optima.
Do not describe a competitive inhibitor as binding somewhere other than the active site.
Do not say increasing substrate concentration raises the rate forever; the rate levels off when active sites are saturated.
In a comparison, do not reverse the models: Lock-and-Key has a fixed active site, while Induced Fit has a changing active site.
